sections.html:
The probate court of the county where the person lived at death. Georgia gives each county's probate court original jurisdiction over wills and the administration of estates, according to the Georgia courts self-help page.

A retired probate judge's layman's guide, posted by Columbia County, tells families that the standard petitions are filled out on forms available at the courthouse and on the Georgia probate courts' website. It also says the forms are built for simple filings, and that anyone who finds the task harder than expected should talk to an attorney. If a house is part of the estate, the probate court is also the place that decides whether the personal representative may sell it.

sections.h2: How does a Georgia probate start when there is a will?
sections.html:
The person named as executor files a petition to probate the will, and the original signed will goes to the court with it. The guide names Standard Form 5 (Petition to Probate Will in Solemn Form) for that purpose, along with Standard Form 6, interrogatories to the will's witness.

Anyone holding a decedent's will must bring it to the probate court for filing, even when nobody plans to probate it. The petition lists the heirs by name, age, address and relationship, and the person signing swears to it before a notary or a probate clerk.

  • File in the county where the decedent was domiciled at death.
  • List every heir, including adopted children and children born outside marriage, but not stepchildren.
  • Expect the court to ask about any other will that someone may be offering elsewhere. The guide says that situation usually calls for an attorney.

sections.h2: What happens in Georgia when there is no will?
sections.html:
The probate judge appoints an administrator, who receives letters of administration showing authority over the estate. The petition is Standard Form 3, and the guide says anyone age 18 or older who is not incapacitated can serve, even if the person lives outside Georgia.

Heirs follow a set order. A surviving spouse and children come first, then parents, then siblings and their descendants, then grandparents, then aunts and uncles and their children, and finally the closest living relatives. A parent who willfully abandoned a minor child can lose that inheritance, though the guide says proving abandonment is work for an attorney.

An administrator normally posts a bond and files reports. If all heirs agree, the court can waive both, but notice of that request must be published in the county newspaper so creditors have a chance to object.

sections.h2: Can the estate's house be sold during Georgia probate?
sections.html:
Yes, but often only after the probate court gives permission. According to the guide, an intestate administrator, a temporary administrator and an executor all need leave to sell unless the will or the beneficiaries granted power to sell without advance approval.

The request for permission is Standard Form 13. The petition describes the property using the legal description from the recorded deed, states why the sale is needed, and says how the sale will happen and the lowest price acceptable. A contract already signed must be attached, and the guide says it should include a clause making the sale subject to court approval.

  • Attach a recent appraisal or the latest ad valorem tax statement for the property.
  • Raise the bond if needed so it covers the net sale proceeds.
  • Give notice to every heir or beneficiary. They may sign a notarized waiver, which the guide describes as far cheaper than sheriff service.
  • If an heir is a minor, incapacitated or cannot be found, the court appoints a guardian ad litem.

Rapid-sale petitions exist only for perishable personal property. Standard Form 15 does not cover a house.

sections.h2: Which Georgia probate petition fits which situation?
sections.html:
The court's standard forms are numbered, and the table below matches them to the situations a family selling inherited property usually faces.

Georgia probate standard forms mentioned in the Columbia County layman's guide
FormUseSource
Form 3Petition for letters of administration (no will)Layman's Guide to Probate
Form 5Petition to probate a will in solemn formSame guide
Form 10Petition for year's supportSame guide
Form 13Personal representative's petition for leave to sell propertySame guide
Form 15Leave to sell perishable personal propertySame guide
Form 17Leave to convey or encumber property set aside as year's supportSame guide

sections.h2: What is year's support in Georgia?
sections.html:
Year's support is an award of estate property to a surviving spouse, to minor children, or to both. It must be requested within 24 months of the date of death, in the probate court of the county where the decedent lived.

The guide lists two reasons families choose it. In many cases the decedent's creditors cannot reach property awarded this way, and a house awarded as year's support may not need back property taxes paid. It can be requested whether or not there is a will, but a spouse who remarried cannot receive it, and a child must be under 18 and unmarried.

Only property the decedent owned at death qualifies. A home held in joint tenancy with right of survivorship passes to the surviving joint owner and cannot be awarded. If no one objects after the hearing, the judge awards the property requested, and the certificate filed in superior court stands in place of a deed. A spouse or guardian who later wants to sell that property files Form 17.

sections.h2: Does Georgia charge an estate or inheritance tax?
sections.html:
No. The Department of Revenue states that Georgia has no inheritance tax and that, since July 1, 2014, the state levies no estate tax and requires no state estate tax return (O.C.G.A. 48-12-1).

The department adds that Georgia has no tax waiver requirement for transferring a decedent's stock or other assets. Anything owed to the IRS is a separate question, so ask the estate's accountant or the IRS whether a federal return applies.

sections.h2: Do transfer-on-death deeds and small-estate rules change the plan?
sections.html:
They can. The Department of Revenue's 2026 legislative update summarizes HB 413 on transfer-on-death deeds: a designated beneficiary has a right to a death certificate, the deed takes priority over unsecured debts, and revoking one now needs a single witness.

The same summary says no PT-61 transfer tax form is filed when the deed is recorded. The form is due only when the beneficiary later records an acceptance affidavit. The update also describes SB 403, which lets property of a deceased person held by the state as unclaimed property go out by affidavit instead of probate when it is under $7,500 and all heirs agree and sign. Ask the probate court clerk and the superior court clerk in the decedent's county how each step is handled locally.

sections.h2: Who pays property tax and transfer tax when an inherited Georgia house sells?
sections.html:
The owner on January 1 owes that year's property tax, and the Department of Revenue says Georgia law allows no refund when a property sells later in the year. Ask the county tax commissioner for the payoff figure before closing.

Real estate transfer tax is a separate charge. The department says it is due before a deed can be recorded with the superior court clerk, that the statute makes the seller liable, and that buyers and sellers often agree by contract who pays. The rate printed on the department's page is $1 for the first $1,000 and 10 cents for each additional $100 or fraction.

faqs.q: Do I need a lawyer to open a Georgia probate case?
faqs.a: Not always. The probate courts publish standard forms meant for simple filings, but the layman's guide says to see an attorney when the filing gets harder than expected, when heirs cannot be found, or when someone disputes a will.

faqs.q: Can an heir sell the inherited house before probate is opened?
faqs.a: Generally no, because the estate, not the heirs, holds title until a personal representative is appointed and any needed court approval is given. Ask the probate clerk in the decedent's county what is required before a buyer or title company will close.

faqs.q: How long can a surviving spouse wait to request year's support?
faqs.a: Twenty-four months from the date of death. The petition is filed in the probate court of the county where the decedent lived, using Standard Form 10.

faqs.q: Does Georgia require the estate to pay a state tax before heirs receive property?
faqs.a: No. The Department of Revenue says Georgia has no estate or inheritance tax and does not require a tax waiver to transfer inherited assets.

faqs.q: Who must be notified when the personal representative asks to sell real estate?
faqs.a: Every heir if there is no will, or every beneficiary if there is a will. They can sign notarized waivers, and the court publishes notice in the county newspaper when an address is unknown.
